common_name: Apalachee Crape Myrtle (Fragrant Light Lavender Cinnamon-Bark Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Set out balled or containerized stock in spring in full sun once hard freezes have passed.

directions: Apalachee stands out among National Arboretum hybrids for its lightly fragrant, soft lavender flower panicles, a rare trait in crape myrtles. Its cinnamon-orange exfoliating bark and dark green, mildew-resistant foliage give it multi-season interest as a small vase-shaped tree. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil and limit pruning to removing crossing branches and spent seed heads in late winter. Once roots are established it shrugs off heat and drought, flowering steadily from midsummer through fall.

common_name: Tuskegee Crape Myrtle (Dark Pink Fluted-Bark Indian-Series Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in an open, sunny site with room for a broad, multi-trunked canopy.

directions: Tuskegee is a broad-spreading Indian-series hybrid prized for its dark pink to near-red blooms that persist for roughly 100 days and for the distinctive fluted grooves in its trunk. Foliage emerges red-tinged before turning glossy dark green and finishing the season in orange-red fall color. It handles both Gulf Coast humidity and the heat of far southern zones better than most cultivars, so give it full sun and let it develop its natural multi-trunk form. Water regularly the first year, then rely on rainfall except during extended drought.

common_name: Lipan Crape Myrtle (Lavender-Pink Smooth-Bark Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Install in spring in full sun with good air movement to keep foliage dry and mildew-free.

directions: Lipan produces frilly, crinkled lavender-pink panicles all summer on new wood, making it a reliable rebloomer if faded clusters are deadheaded. The smooth bark becomes more visible as the plant matures and drops its dark green leaves, which turn orange and red in autumn. Site it in full sun with well-drained soil; it tolerates heat and drought well once established. Prune minimally in late winter, thinning crowded interior growth rather than heading back the canopy.

common_name: Chickasaw Crape Myrtle (True Dwarf Mounded Lavender-Pink Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in a container, border edge, or rock garden where its tight mounded form can be appreciated up close.

directions: Chickasaw is one of the smallest true crape myrtles available, forming a dense, mounded dwarf shrub rather than a tree. Glossy red buds open to pinkish-lavender flowers from midsummer to frost, and the dark foliage turns bronze-red in autumn. Because of its miniature scale it excels in containers, foundation plantings, and small-space borders in full sun. It needs little pruning beyond removing spent flower clusters and rarely requires supplemental water once established.

common_name: Caddo Crape Myrtle (Semi-Dwarf Bright Pink Cinnamon-Bark Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Set plants in spring in full sun where a low, spreading semi-dwarf habit fits foundation or border plantings.

directions: Caddo grows as a low, spreading semi-dwarf shrub with excellent field tolerance to powdery mildew and abundant bright pink flower panicles from midsummer into September. Exfoliating bark reveals light cinnamon-brown wood beneath, adding cold-season interest after leaf drop. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil and space plants to allow air circulation between them. Light structural pruning in late winter is all it needs; avoid hard topping, which sacrifices its naturally graceful spreading form.

common_name: Powhatan Crape Myrtle (Violet-Purple Cold-Hardy Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun; its cold hardiness makes it a good choice for the cooler end of crape myrtle range.

directions: Powhatan is a National Arboretum introduction bred from dwarf purple parent lines, giving it unusually saturated violet-purple flower clusters on an upright, broadly rounded frame. It can be trained as a large shrub or limbed up into a small tree, with exfoliating bark and orange-to-red fall foliage adding off-season appeal. Grow in full sun on average, well-drained soil; it is notably cold hardy and disease resistant compared to older indica selections. Prune selectively in late winter to shape rather than shear, preserving its natural branching habit.

common_name: Delta Moonlight Crape Myrtle (White-Flowered Dark Burgundy Foliage Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun so the dark burgundy leaves color up well and set off the white flower clusters.

directions: Delta Moonlight pairs crisp white summer-to-fall blooms with dark burgundy foliage that holds its color even through peak summer heat, part of the Southern Living Delta series bred for disease resistance. Its upright, vase-shaped habit suits it to specimen use or narrow side-yard plantings. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil; it reblooms readily if spent panicles are removed. Once established it is drought and pest tolerant, needing water mainly during prolonged dry spells.

common_name: Black Diamond Best Red Crape Myrtle (Dark Foliage Medium-Red Reblooming Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun; foliage color and flower intensity are both strongest in strong direct light.

directions: Best Red sits between its Black Diamond series siblings in both habit and bloom intensity, offering a medium red flower color on near-black purple foliage that holds its tone through the growing season. It flowers continuously from late spring through fall with light deadheading of spent panicles. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil; the dark leaves show best contrast against light-colored walls or fencing. Established plants are drought tolerant and need minimal pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood in late winter.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection / Black Diamond series

common_name: Black Diamond Crimson Red Crape Myrtle (Dark Foliage Shrubby Bright Red Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun; its naturally shrubbier habit suits mixed borders as well as specimen use.

directions: Crimson Red carries the brightest red flowers of the Black Diamond series set against near-black purple foliage, and it naturally grows into a fuller, shrubbier form than its tree-like siblings. It blooms in flushes from summer through fall, reblooming best when faded panicles are trimmed off. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil for the darkest leaf color and heaviest flowering. Once rooted in it tolerates heat and drought well, and pruning can be limited to light late-winter shaping.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection / Black Diamond series

common_name: Black Diamond Pure White Crape Myrtle (Dark Foliage Upright White-Flowered Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun and allow room for the most upright, tree-like habit of the Black Diamond series.

directions: Pure White is the most tree-like selection in the Black Diamond series, growing into a strongly upright form that shows off crisp white flower clusters against near-black purple-black leaves. It flowers repeatedly from late spring through fall and takes readily to training as a single- or multi-trunk specimen. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil for the deepest foliage color and best bloom set. It is heat and drought tolerant once established, needing only light corrective pruning in late winter.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection / Black Diamond series

common_name: Moonlight Magic Crape Myrtle (Purple-Maroon Foliage White-Flowered Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun so the purple-maroon leaves develop maximum color contrast with the white blooms.

directions: Moonlight Magic, part of the First Editions Magic series, holds rich purple-maroon foliage through the heat of summer and sets it off with bright white flower clusters in late July and August. Its compact, upright habit fits foundation plantings and mixed borders where dark foliage color is wanted without a large mature footprint. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; deadhead spent panicles to encourage a second flush of bloom. It tolerates heat and drought once established and needs only minor late-winter pruning to maintain shape.

common_name: Plum Magic Crape Myrtle (Plum-Purple Foliage Fuchsia-Pink Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun; new foliage emerges plum-purple before maturing to dark green as the season progresses.

directions: Plum Magic opens the season with plum-purple new growth that gradually matures to rich dark green, providing a shifting foliage backdrop for its abundant fuchsia-pink flower clusters in early summer. Its upright, rounded form works well as a small specimen tree or large accent shrub. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil for the strongest foliage color and heaviest bloom. Once established it needs little more than occasional deep watering during drought and light shaping in late winter.
